title: Learning the Entropic Relaxation: Stable Coarse-Grid Emulation with Neural Discrete Equilibrium
claim: Coarse discretization removes the dissipative tail of the energy cascade, so unresolved energy piles up as grid-scale noise unless modeled.
layout: 3x3 grid of spectra; columns time, rows resolution; Nyquist shading and glyphs
description: A 3x3 grid of log-log energy spectrum plots. Columns are Early time, Developed turbulence and Late time. Rows are Turbulence cascade, Coarse graining and Very coarse graining. The top row shows a gray resolved reference curve under a dashed k^-5/3 line. Blue swirl icons of shrinking size run along the line to show the energy cascade. In the lower rows a beige shaded region marks wavenumbers beyond the Nyquist limit, with a dashed orange vertical line and a small orange monster icon at the cutoff. The unstabilized blue curve rises and oscillates near the cutoff, and the oscillation grows more severe at later times and coarser grids. The black entropy-stabilized curve follows the reference and then drops off at the cutoff. A legend runs across the top. The eye goes first to the blue spikes near the monster icons.
caption: Coarse discretization interrupts scale-to-scale energy transfer. Solid curves show the resolved spectral power at successive stages of a rollout; dashed lines indicate an idealized inertial-range decay. As turbulence develops, a coarse representation loses the high-wavenumber dissipative tail and can accumulate grid-scale content, unless the unresolved transfer is modeled. The learned entropic relaxation supplies a local dissipative channel for this missing transfer.
abstract: The ability to emulate complicated and computationally-expensive physical systems in an efficient and stable manner is a popular motivation for scientific machine learning (SciML). Stable numerical solvers tend to be computationally expensive, as they attempt to resolve small (spatial and temporal) scales that receive and dissipate spectral energy. Learned coarse-grid forecasters remove the dissipative channel, allowing unresolved frequencies to re-emerge as grid-scale noise (aliasing). In this paper, we use the Neural Discrete Equilibrium (NeurDE) method to explore stable emulation at extremely coarse grids, demonstrating physically-principled control over entropy dynamics that reinforces the physical system's dissipative mechanism. Entropically-stabilized NeurDE produces stable long-time rollouts for thousands of forecasting steps on large Reynolds number turbulent flows ($\mathrm{Re}=100{,}000$) with very coarse grids (down to $\mathbb{R}^{16\times16}$). At these very coarse grid scales, entropically-stabilized NeurDE can be more stable than even our stabilized data-generation numerical method.
